**Seoul** (/soʊl/; [Korean](Korean_language "Korean language"): 서울; Korean: [sʌul] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/7d/Ko-Seoul.ogg/Ko-Seoul.ogg.mp3)i; lit. (literal translation) 'Capital'), officially **Seoul Special City**, is the capital and largest metropolis of South Korea. It forms the heart of the [Seoul Capital Area](Seoul_Capital_Area "Seoul Capital Area"), which also includes the surrounding <Incheon> metropolis and [Gyeonggi Province](Gyeonggi_Province "Gyeonggi Province"). Considered a [global city](Global_city "Global city") and rated as an Alpha city by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") (GaWC),[[9]](Seoul#cite_note-9) Seoul was the world's [fourth-largest metropolitan economy](List_of_cities_by_GDP "List of cities by GDP") in 2014, following <Tokyo>, [New York City](New_York_City "New York City"), and [Los Angeles](Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").

Seoul was the capital of various Korean states, including <Baekje>, <Joseon>, the [Korean Empire](Korean_Empire "Korean Empire"), <Goryeo> (as a secondary capital), and presently South Korea. It is strategically located along the [Han River](Han_River_(Korea) "Han River (Korea)"). Seoul's history stretches back over two thousand years, when it was founded in 18 BC by the people of Baekje, one of the [Three Kingdoms of Korea](Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea "Three Kingdoms of Korea"). The city was later designated the capital of Korea under the Joseon dynasty. The city was ringed by the [Fortress Wall of Seoul](Fortress_Wall_of_Seoul "Fortress Wall of Seoul") during the Joseon period. The [Empire of Japan](Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") occupied Seoul from 1910 to 1945 and renamed it "<Gyeongseong>." During the [Korean War](Korean_War "Korean War") (1950–1953), Seoul saw fierce fighting and changed hands four times, leaving the city mostly destroyed. Seoul has since been rebuilt and rapidly urbanized.

Seoul was rated Asia's most livable city with the second highest quality of life globally by <Arcadis> in 2015, with a [GDP per capita (PPP)](List_of_South_Korean_regions_by_GDP "List of South Korean regions by GDP") of around $40,000. With major technology hubs centered in <Gangnam> and [Digital Media City](Digital_Media_City "Digital Media City"),[[10]](Seoul#cite_note-10) the Seoul Capital Area is home to the headquarters of 15 [*Fortune* Global 500](Fortune_Global_500 "Fortune Global 500") companies, including <Samsung>,[[11]](Seoul#cite_note-11) <LG>, and [Hyundai](Hyundai_Motor_Group "Hyundai Motor Group"). Ranked seventh in the [Global Power City Index](Global_city "Global city") and [Global Financial Centres Index](Global_Financial_Centres_Index "Global Financial Centres Index"), the metropolis exerts a major influence in global affairs as one of the five leading [hosts of global conferences](Union_of_International_Associations "Union of International Associations").[[12]](Seoul#cite_note-12) Seoul has hosted the [1986 Asian Games](1986_Asian_Games "1986 Asian Games"), the [1988 Summer Olympics](1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics"), and the [2010 G20 Seoul summit](2010_G20_Seoul_summit "2010 G20 Seoul summit").

Seoul is surrounded by a mountainous and hilly landscape, with [Bukhan Mountain](Bukhansan "Bukhansan") located on the northern edge of the city. The Seoul Capital Area contains five UNESCO [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"): [Changdeok Palace](Changdeokgung "Changdeokgung"), [Hwaseong Fortress](Hwaseong_Fortress "Hwaseong Fortress"), [Jongmyo Shrine](Jongmyo_(Seoul) "Jongmyo (Seoul)"), <Namhansanseong>, and the [Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty](Royal_Tombs_of_the_Joseon_dynasty "Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty").[[13]](Seoul#cite_note-13) More recently, Seoul has been a major site of modern architectural construction; major modern landmarks include the [N Seoul Tower](N_Seoul_Tower "N Seoul Tower"), the [63 Building](63_Building "63 Building"), the [Lotte World Tower](Lotte_World_Tower "Lotte World Tower"), the [Dongdaemun Design Plaza](Dongdaemun_Design_Plaza "Dongdaemun Design Plaza"), [Lotte World](Lotte_World "Lotte World"), the [Trade Tower](Trade_Tower "Trade Tower"), [COEX](World_Trade_Center_Seoul "World Trade Center Seoul"), [IFC Seoul](International_Finance_Center_Seoul "International Finance Center Seoul"), and <Parc1>. Seoul was named the [2010 World Design Capital](World_Design_Capital "World Design Capital"). It is the birthplace of <K-pop> and the [Korean Wave](Korean_Wave "Korean Wave"), as the city is a center for Korean culture with numerous entertainment companies.

## Toponomy

Main article: [Names of Seoul](Names_of_Seoul "Names of Seoul")

The city has been known in the past by the names <Wiryeseong> (위례성; 慰禮城, during the <Baekje> era), Bukhansangun (북한산군; 北漢山郡 during the <Goguryeo> era), Namcheon (남천; 南川,[[14]](Seoul#cite_note-Jinheung_Taewang_Stele_Seoul-14) during the <Silla> era), [Hanyang](History_of_Seoul "History of Seoul") (한양; 漢陽, during the [Northern and Southern States period](Northern_and_Southern_States_period "Northern and Southern States period")), Namgyeong(남경; 南京, during <Goryeo> era), Hanseong (한성; 漢城, during the <Joseon> era), and [Keijō](Keij%C5%8D "Keijō") (京城) or Gyeongseong (경성; 京城) during Japanese rule.[[15]](Seoul#cite_note-Encyclopædia_Britannica-15)

During [Japan's annexation of Korea](Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule"), *Hanseong* (漢城) was renamed *Keijō* (京城) by the Imperial authorities to prevent confusion with the <Hanja> '[漢](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/漢 "wikt:漢")' (a transliteration of an ancient Korean word *Han* ([한](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/한 "wikt:한")) meaning "great"), which also refers to Han people or the [Han dynasty](Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") in Chinese and in Japanese is a term for "China".[[16]](Seoul#cite_note-16)

After [World War II](World_War_II "World War II") and the [liberation of Korea](Surrender_of_Japan "Surrender of Japan"), the city took its present name, which originated from the [Korean](Korean_language "Korean language") word meaning "capital city", which is believed to have descended from an ancient word, *Seorabeol* (서라벌; 徐羅伐), which originally referred to <Gyeongju>, the capital of <Silla>.[[17]](Seoul#cite_note-17) Ancient Gyeongju was also known in documents by the Chinese-style name *Geumseong* (金城, literally "Gold Castle or City" or "Metal Castle or City"), but it is unclear whether the native Korean-style name *Seorabeol* had the same meaning as *Geumseong*.

Unlike most place names in Korea, "Seoul" has no corresponding <Hanja> ([Chinese characters](Chinese_characters "Chinese characters") used in the Korean language). On 18 January 2005, the Seoul government changed its official name in Chinese characters from the historic *Hancheng* ([simplified Chinese](Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 汉城; [traditional Chinese](Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 漢城; [pinyin](Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Hànchéng*) to *Shou'er* (首尔; 首爾; *Shǒu'ěr*).[[18]](Seoul#cite_note-18)[[19]](Seoul#cite_note-19)

## History

Main article: [History of Seoul](History_of_Seoul "History of Seoul")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Seoul](Timeline_of_Seoul "Timeline of Seoul").

### Early history

Settlement of the [Han River](Han_River_(Korea) "Han River (Korea)") area, where present-day Seoul is located, began around 4000 BC.[[20]](Seoul#cite_note-Britannica-20)

Seoul is first recorded as Wiryeseong, the capital of <Baekje> (founded in 18 BC) in the northeastern area of modern Seoul.[[20]](Seoul#cite_note-Britannica-20) There are several city walls remaining in the area that date from this time. <Pungnaptoseong>, an earthen wall located southeast Seoul, is widely believed to have been at the main Wiryeseong site.[[21]](Seoul#cite_note-toseong-21) As the Three Kingdoms competed for this strategic region, control passed from Baekje to <Goguryeo> in the 5th century.[[22]](Seoul#cite_note-22)

However, according to Samguk Sagi, both Baekje and Silla described the land as frontier border of Baekje, not as the capital region.[[23]](Seoul#cite_note-Samguk_Sagi_Silla_Jinheung_19-23)[[24]](Seoul#cite_note-Samguk_Sagi_Baekje_Seong_19-24) Moreover, Jinheung Taewang Stele found at current day <Bukhansan> tells that the place was underdeveloped as of 6th century AD,[[14]](Seoul#cite_note-Jinheung_Taewang_Stele_Seoul-14) suggesting that the first capital Wiryeseong was not located in or nearby Seoul.

In July or August 553, <Silla> took the control of the region from Baekje, and the city became a part of newly established Sin Province (신주; 新州).[[23]](Seoul#cite_note-Samguk_Sagi_Silla_Jinheung_19-23)[[24]](Seoul#cite_note-Samguk_Sagi_Baekje_Seong_19-24) Sin (新) has both meaning of "New" and "Silla", thus literally means New Silla Province.

In November 555, Jinheung Taewang made royal visit to Bukhansan, and inspected the borderline.[[25]](Seoul#cite_note-25) In 557, Silla abolished Sin Province, and established Bukhansan Province (북한산주; 北漢山州).[[26]](Seoul#cite_note-26) The word Hanseong (한성; 漢城; lit. (literal translation) Han Fortress) appears on the stone wall of "Pyongyang Fortress", which was presumably built in the mid to late 6th century AD over period of 42 years, located in Pyongyang, while there is no evidence that Seoul had name Hanseong dating the three kingdoms and earlier period.[[27]](Seoul#cite_note-27)[[28]](Seoul#cite_note-28)[[29]](Seoul#cite_note-29)[[30]](Seoul#cite_note-30)[[31]](Seoul#cite_note-31)

The **Seoul Capital Area** (**SCA**; [Korean](Korean_language "Korean language"): 수도권, [sʰu.do.k͈wʌ̹n]) or **Gyeonggi region** (경기 지방), is the metropolitan area of <Seoul>, <Incheon>, and [Gyeonggi Province](Gyeonggi_Province "Gyeonggi Province"), located in north-west South Korea. Its population of 26 million (as of 2020)[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_Capital_Area#endnote_ppl) is ranked as the [fourth largest metropolitan area](List_of_metropolitan_areas_by_population "List of metropolitan areas by population") in the world. Its area is about 12,685 km2 (4,898 sq mi). It forms the cultural, commercial, financial, industrial, and residential center of South Korea. The largest city is Seoul, with a population of approximately 10 million people, followed by Incheon, with 3 million inhabitants.

## Geography and climate

See also: [Geography of South Korea](Geography_of_South_Korea "Geography of South Korea")

The Capital Area occupies a plain in the [Han River](Han_River_(Korea) "Han River (Korea)") valley.[[4]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-4)

## History

See also: [History of South Korea](History_of_South_Korea "History of South Korea") and [History of Seoul](History_of_Seoul "History of Seoul")

## Demographics

See also: [Demographics of South Korea](Demographics_of_South_Korea "Demographics of South Korea")

Covering only about 12% of the country's area, the Seoul Capital Area is home to more than 48.2% of the national population, and is the world's [ninth largest urban area](List_of_urban_areas_by_population "List of urban areas by population"). This percentage has risen steadily since the mid-20th century, and the trend is expected to continue. Currently more than half of the people who move from one region to another are moving to the capital area.[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_Capital_Area#endnote_trend1) In 2020, it was reported that the Seoul Capital Area's population had exceeded 50% of the country's total population, with 25,925,799 people living in the area (50.002% of the total 51,849,861).[[5]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-5)

## Economy

See also: [Economy of South Korea](Economy_of_South_Korea "Economy of South Korea") and Category:Companies based in Seoul

In 2017, Seoul Capital Area's gross regional product was ₩870 trillion([US$](US%24 "US$")770 billion), generating half of the country's total <GDP>.[[6]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-6) It is the fourth largest urban economy in the world after Tokyo, New York City and Los Angeles,[[7]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-7) and the region hosts headquarters of 59 [Forbes Global 2000](Forbes_Global_2000 "Forbes Global 2000") companies.[[8]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-8) As the economy of Seoul Capital Area transformed to [knowledge economy](Knowledge_economy "Knowledge economy") from the [manufacturing](Manufacturing "Manufacturing")-based economy of the 20th century, there are a number of high-tech business parks in Seoul Capital Area, such as [Digital Media City](Digital_Media_City "Digital Media City") and [Pangyo Techno Valley](Pangyo_Techno_Valley "Pangyo Techno Valley").

The Seoul Capital Area is home to the most affluent and livable cities and apartments in Korea but there are significant discrepancies between cities and districts, particularly between those built in the older and newer generations. Newer areas with more modern and luxurious apartments and infrastructure are more expensive, along with proximity to [Gangnam District](Gangnam_District "Gangnam District"), the commercial center of the region.[[9]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-9)

## Government

See also: [Government of South Korea](Government_of_South_Korea "Government of South Korea")

Various agencies have been set up to deal with the intergovernmental problems of the region. Proposals for consolidating some or all of the cities of the capital area into a handful of metropolitan cities have thus far not been implemented.

Development in the area is currently governed by the Capital Region Readjustment Planning Act (수도권정비계획법), first passed in 1982 and last revised in 1996.

## Subdivisions

See also: [Administrative divisions of South Korea](Administrative_divisions_of_South_Korea "Administrative divisions of South Korea")

The Seoul Capital Area is divided among the special city of <Seoul>, the metropolitan city of <Incheon>, and province of [Gyeonggi](Gyeonggi_Province "Gyeonggi Province"). Seoul has 25 gu (local government wards),[[10]](Seoul_Capital_Area#cite_note-10) Incheon has 8 gu and 2 counties, and Gyeonggi Province has 28 cities and 3 counties as the subdivisions.

## Geography

Pyongyang is in the west-central part of North Korea; the city lies on a flat plain about 50 kilometres (31 mi) east of the [Korea Bay](Korea_Bay "Korea Bay"), an arm of the [Yellow Sea](Yellow_Sea "Yellow Sea"). The [Taedong River](Taedong_River "Taedong River") flows southwestward through the city toward the Korea Bay. The Pyongyang plain, where the city is situated, is one of the two large plains on the Western coast of the Korean peninsula, the other being the Chaeryong plain. Both have an area of approximately 500 square kilometers.[[62]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200963-64)

### Climate

Pyongyang has a hot-summer [humid continental climate](Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") ([Köppen](K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): *Dwa*), featuring warm to hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters.[[63]](Pyongyang#cite_note-65)[[64]](Pyongyang#cite_note-66) Cold, dry winds can blow from [Siberia](Siberian_High "Siberian High") in winter, making conditions very cold; the low temperature is usually below freezing between November and early March, although the average daytime high is at least a few degrees above freezing in every month except January. The winter is generally much drier than summer, with snow falling for 37 days on average.

The transition from the cold, dry winter to the warm, wet summer occurs rather quickly between April and early May, and there is a similarly abrupt return to winter conditions in late October and November. Summers are generally hot and humid, with the [East Asian monsoon](East_Asian_monsoon "East Asian monsoon") taking place from June until September; these are also the hottest months, with average temperatures of 21 to 25 °C (70 to 77 °F), and daytime highs often above 30 °C (86 °F). Although largely transitional seasons, spring and autumn experience more pleasant weather, with average high temperatures ranging from 20 to 26 °C (68 to 79 °F) in May and 22 to 27 °C (72 to 81 °F) in September,[[65]](Pyongyang#cite_note-67)[[66]](Pyongyang#cite_note-68) coupled with relatively clear, sunny skies.[[67]](Pyongyang#cite_note-69)[[68]](Pyongyang#cite_note-70)

## Politics

Major government and other public offices are located in Pyongyang, which is constitutionally designated as the country's capital.[[73]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study2009196-75) The [seat](Government_Complex_No._1%2C_Pyongyang "Government Complex No. 1, Pyongyang") of the [Workers' Party Central Committee](Central_Committee_of_the_Workers'_Party_of_Korea "Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea") and the Pyongyang People's Committee are located in Haebangsan-dong, <Chung-guyok>. The [Cabinet of North Korea](Cabinet_of_North_Korea "Cabinet of North Korea") is located in Jongro-dong, <Chung-guyok>.

Pyongyang is also the seat of all major North Korean security institutions. The largest of them, the [Ministry of People's Security](Ministry_of_Social_Security_(North_Korea) "Ministry of Social Security (North Korea)"), has 130,000 employees working in 12 bureaus. These oversee activities including: police services, security of party officials, classified documents, census, civil registrations, large-scale public construction, [traffic control](Traffic_control "Traffic control"), fire safety, [civil defence](Civil_defence "Civil defence"), [public health](Public_health "Public health") and [customs](Customs "Customs").[[74]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study2009276–277-76) Another significant structure based in the city is the [State Security Department](Ministry_of_State_Security_(North_Korea) "Ministry of State Security (North Korea)"), whose 30,000 personnel manage intelligence, political prison systems, military industrial security and entry and exit management.[[75]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study2009277-77)

The politics and management of the city is dominated by the [Workers' Party of Korea](Workers'_Party_of_Korea "Workers' Party of Korea"), as they are in the national level. The city is managed by the Pyongyang Party Committee of the [Workers' Party of Korea](Workers'_Party_of_Korea "Workers' Party of Korea") and its chairman is the *de facto* [mayor](Mayor "Mayor"). The supreme standing state organ is the Pyongyang People's Committee, responsible
for everyday events in support of the city. This includes following local Party guidance as channeled through the Pyongyang Party Committee, the distribution of resources prioritised to Pyongyang, and providing support to KWP and internal security agency personnel and families.

## Cityscape

Panorama of Pyongyang, as seen from the *Juche* Tower in April 2012

After being destroyed during the Korean War, Pyongyang was entirely rebuilt according to Kim Il Sung's vision, which was to create a capital that would boost morale in the post-war years.[[81]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200991,93–94-83) The result was a city with wide, tree-lined [boulevards](Boulevard "Boulevard") and public buildings with terraced landscaping, [mosaics](Mosaic "Mosaic") and decorated ceilings.[[82]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200991-84) Its Russian-style architecture makes it reminiscent of a [Siberian](Siberia "Siberia") city during winter snowfall, although edifices of traditional Korean design somewhat soften this perception. In summer, it is notable for its rivers, willow trees, flowers and parkland.[[82]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200991-84)

The streets are laid out in a north–south, east–west grid, giving the city an orderly appearance.[[82]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200991-84) North Korean designers applied the Swedish experience of self-sufficient urban neighbourhoods throughout the entire country, and Pyongyang is no exception. Its inhabitants are mostly divided into administrative units of 5,000 to 6,000 people (*dong*). These units all have similar sets of amenities including a food store, a barber shop, a [tailor](Tailor "Tailor"), a public bathhouse, a [post office](Post_office "Post office"), a clinic, a library and others. Many residents occupy high-rise apartment buildings.[[83]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200997-85) One of Kim Il Sung's priorities while designing Pyongyang was to limit the population. Authorities maintain a restrictive regime of movement into the city, making it atypical of [East Asia](East_Asia "East Asia") as it is silent, uncrowded and spacious.[[84]](Pyongyang#cite_note-FOOTNOTECountry_Study200991-92-86)

Structures in Pyongyang are divided into three major architectural categories: monuments, buildings with traditional Korean motifs and high-rises.[[85]](Pyongyang#cite_note-LCCS93-87) Some of North Korea's most recognisable landmarks are monuments, like the [*Juche* Tower](Juche_Tower "Juche Tower"), the [Arch of Triumph](Arch_of_Triumph_(Pyongyang) "Arch of Triumph (Pyongyang)") and the [Mansu Hill Grand Monument](Mansu_Hill_Grand_Monument "Mansu Hill Grand Monument"). The first of them is a 170-meter (560 ft) [granite](Granite "Granite") spire symbolizing the *<Juche>* ideology. It was completed in 1982 and contains 25,550 granite blocks, one for each day of Kim Il Sung's life up to that point.[[85]](Pyongyang#cite_note-LCCS93-87) The most prominent building on Pyongyang's skyline is [Ryugyong Hotel](Ryugyong_Hotel "Ryugyong Hotel"),[[85]](Pyongyang#cite_note-LCCS93-87) the [seventh highest building](List_of_buildings_with_100_floors_or_more "List of buildings with 100 floors or more") in the world terms of floor count, the tallest unoccupied building in the world,[[86]](Pyongyang#cite_note-88) and one of the [tallest hotels in the world](List_of_tallest_hotels_in_the_world "List of tallest hotels in the world"). It has yet to open.[[87]](Pyongyang#cite_note-89)[[88]](Pyongyang#cite_note-bloom-90)

Pyongyang has a rapidly evolving skyline, dominated by high-rise apartment buildings. A construction boom began with the Changjon Street Apartment Complex, which was completed in 2012.[[89]](Pyongyang#cite_note-CityLab-91) Construction of the complex began after late leader [Kim Jong Il](Kim_Jong_Il "Kim Jong Il") described Changjon Street as "pitiful".[[90]](Pyongyang#cite_note-92) Other housing complexes are being upgraded as well, but most are still poorly insulated, and lacking elevators and central heating.[[91]](Pyongyang#cite_note-93) An urban renewal program continued under Kim Jong Un's leadership, with the old apartments of the 1970s and '80s replaced by taller high rise buildings and leisure parks like the [Kaesong Youth Park](Kaeson_Youth_Park "Kaeson Youth Park"), as well as renovations of older buildings.[[92]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Makinen-94) In 2018, the city was described as unrecognizable compared to five years before.[[93]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Salmon-95)

## Culture

### Cuisine

See also: [North Korean cuisine](North_Korean_cuisine "North Korean cuisine")

Pyongyang served as the provincial capital of [South Pyongan Province](South_Pyongan_Province "South Pyongan Province") until 1946,[[94]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EncyKorea_Pyongyang-96) and Pyongyang cuisine shares the general culinary tradition of the Pyongan province. The most famous local food is *[Pyongyang raengmyŏn](Pyongyang_naengmyeon "Pyongyang naengmyeon")*, or also called *mul raengmyŏn* or just simply *raengmyŏn*. *Raengmyŏn* literally means "cold noodles", while the affix *mul* refers to water because the dish is served in a cold broth. *Raengmyŏn* consists of thin and chewy buckwheat noodles in a cold meat-broth with *[dongchimi](Dongchimi "Dongchimi")* (watery kimchi) and topped with a slice of sweet [Korean pear](Korean_pear "Korean pear").

Pyongyang *raengmyŏn* was originally eaten in homes built with *[ondol](Ondol "Ondol")* (traditional [underfloor heating](Underfloor_heating "Underfloor heating")) during the cold winter, so it is also called *"Pyongyang deoldeori"* (shivering in Pyongyang). Pyongyang locals sometimes enjoyed it as a *[haejangguk](Haejangguk "Haejangguk")*, which is any type of food eaten as a hangover cure, usually a warm soup.[[95]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Korean_Portal-97)

Another representative Pyongyang dish, *[Taedonggang sungeoguk](Taedonggang_sungeoguk "Taedonggang sungeoguk")*, translates as "flathead grey mullet soup from the [Taedong River](Taedong_River "Taedong River")". The soup features [flathead grey mullet](Flathead_grey_mullet "Flathead grey mullet") (abundant in the Taedong River) along with black peppercorns and salt.[[96]](Pyongyang#cite_note-98) Traditionally, it has been served to guests visiting Pyongyang. Therefore, there is a common saying, "How good was the trout soup?", which is used to greet people returning from Pyongyang. Another local specialty, *Pyongyang onban* (literally "warm rice of Pyongyang") comprises freshly cooked rice topped with sliced mushrooms, chicken, and a couple of *[bindaetteok](Bindaetteok "Bindaetteok")* (pancakes made from ground mung beans and vegetables).[[95]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Korean_Portal-97)

## Sports

Pyongyang has a number of sports clubs, including the [April 25 Sports Club](April_25_Sports_Club "April 25 Sports Club") and the [Pyongyang City Sports Club](Pyongyang_City_Sports_Club "Pyongyang City Sports Club").[[99]](Pyongyang#cite_note-101)

## Economy

Pyongyang is North Korea's industrial center.[[12]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EBPyongyang-12) Thanks to the abundance of natural resources like [coal](Coal "Coal"), [iron](Iron "Iron") and [limestone](Limestone "Limestone"), as well as good land and water transport systems, it was the first industrial city to emerge in North Korea after the Korean War. Light and heavy industries are both present and have developed in parallel. Heavy manufactures include [cement](Cement "Cement"), industrial ceramics,[[41]](Pyongyang#cite_note-britannica.com-43) munitions and weapons, but mechanical engineering remains the core industry. Light industries in Pyongyang and its vicinity include [textiles](Textiles "Textiles"), footwear and food, among others.[[41]](Pyongyang#cite_note-britannica.com-43) Special emphasis is put on the production and supply of fresh produce and subsidiary crops in farms on the city's outskirts. Other crops include [rice](Rice "Rice"), [sweetcorn](Maize "Maize") and [soybeans](Soybeans "Soybeans"). Pyongyang aims to achieve self-sufficiency in meat production. High-density facilities raise pigs, chicken and other livestock.[[12]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EBPyongyang-12)

Until the late 2010s Pyongyang still experienced frequent shortages of electricity.[[100]](Pyongyang#cite_note-IFES1-102) To solve this problem, two power stations – Huichon Power Stations 1 and 2 – were built in [Chagang Province](Chagang_Province "Chagang Province") and supply the city through direct transmission lines. A second phase of the power expansion project was launched in January 2013, consisting of a series of small dams along the [Chongchon River](Chongchon_River "Chongchon River"). The first two power stations have a maximum generating capacity of 300 megawatts (MW), while the 10 dams to be built under second phase are expected to generate about 120 MW.[[100]](Pyongyang#cite_note-IFES1-102) In addition, the city has several existing or planned [thermal power stations](Thermal_power_station "Thermal power station"). These include Pyongyang TPS with a capacity of 500 MW, East Pyongyang TPS with a capacity of 50 MW, and Kangdong TPS which is under construction.[[101]](Pyongyang#cite_note-103)

### Retail

Pyongyang is home to several large department stores including the [Pothonggang Department Store](Pothonggang_Department_Store "Pothonggang Department Store"), [Pyongyang Department Store No. 1](Pyongyang_Department_Store_No._1 "Pyongyang Department Store No. 1"), Pyongyang Department Store No. 2, Kwangbok Department Store, Ragwon Department Store, Pyongyang Station Department Store, and the Pyongyang Children's Department Store.[[102]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Pyongyang_Metro-104)

The city also has Hwanggumbol Shop, a chain of state-owned convenience stores supplying goods at prices cheaper than those in the [jangmadang](Jangmadang "Jangmadang") markets. Hwanggumbol Shops are specifically designed to control North Korea's expanding markets by attracting consumers and guaranteeing the circulation of money in government-operated stores.[[103]](Pyongyang#cite_note-105)

### Transportation

Pyongyang is also the main transport hub of the country: it has a network of roads, railways and air routes which link it to both foreign and domestic destinations. It is the starting point of inter-regional highways reaching Nampo, Wonsan and Kaesong.[[12]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EBPyongyang-12) [Pyongyang railway station](Pyongyang_Station "Pyongyang Station") serves the main railway lines, including the [Pyongui Line](Pyongui_Line "Pyongui Line") and the [Pyongbu Line](Pyongbu_Line "Pyongbu Line"). Regular international rail services to <Beijing>, the Chinese border city of <Dandong> and <Moscow> are also available.

A rail journey to Beijing takes about 25 hours and 25 minutes (K27 from Beijing/K28 from Pyongyang, on Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays); a journey to Dandong takes about 6 hours (daily); a journey to Moscow takes six days. The city also connects to the [Eurasian Land Bridge](Eurasian_Land_Bridge "Eurasian Land Bridge") via the [Trans-Siberian Railway](Trans-Siberian_Railway "Trans-Siberian Railway"). A [high-speed rail](High-speed_rail "High-speed rail") link to Wonsan is planned.[[104]](Pyongyang#cite_note-106)

The [Metro](Pyongyang_Metro "Pyongyang Metro"), [tram](Pyongyang_tram_system "Pyongyang tram system") and [trolleybus systems](Trolleybuses_in_Pyongyang "Trolleybuses in Pyongyang") are used mainly by commuters as a primary means of urban transportation.[[12]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EBPyongyang-12) Cycle lanes were introduced on main thoroughfares in July 2015.[[105]](Pyongyang#cite_note-107) There are relatively few [cars](Car "Car") in the city. Cars are a symbol of status in the country due to their scarcity as a result of restrictions on import because of international sanctions and domestic regulations.[[106]](Pyongyang#cite_note-108) Some roads are also reported to be in poor condition.[[107]](Pyongyang#cite_note-109) However, by 2018, Pyongyang had begun to experience traffic jams.[[93]](Pyongyang#cite_note-Salmon-95)

State-owned [Air Koryo](Air_Koryo "Air Koryo") has scheduled international flights from [Pyongyang Sunan International Airport](Pyongyang_Sunan_International_Airport "Pyongyang Sunan International Airport") to Beijing ([PEK](Beijing_Capital_International_Airport "Beijing Capital International Airport")), <Shenyang> ([SHE](Shenyang_Taoxian_International_Airport "Shenyang Taoxian International Airport")), <Vladivostok> ([VVO](Vladivostok_Airport "Vladivostok Airport")), <Shanghai> ([PVG](Pudong_International_Airport "Pudong International Airport")) and <Dandong>.[[108]](Pyongyang#cite_note-110) The only domestic destinations are <Hamhung>, <Wonsan>, <Chongjin>, <Hyesan> and <Samjiyon>. Since 31 March 2008, [Air China](Air_China "Air China") launched a regular service between Beijing and Pyongyang,[[109]](Pyongyang#cite_note-111) although Air China's flights are often canceled due to lack of passengers.[[110]](Pyongyang#cite_note-112)

## Education and science

[Kim Il Sung University](Kim_Il_Sung_University "Kim Il Sung University"), North Korea's oldest university, was established in 1946.[[12]](Pyongyang#cite_note-EBPyongyang-12) It has 21 faculties, 4 research institutes, and 10 other university units.[[111]](Pyongyang#cite_note-113)[[112]](Pyongyang#cite_note-114)[[113]](Pyongyang#cite_note-115) These include the primary medical education and health personnel training unit, the medical college; a physics faculty which covers a range of studies including [theoretical physics](Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics"), optical science, [geophysics](Geophysics "Geophysics") and [astrophysics](Astrophysics "Astrophysics");[[114]](Pyongyang#cite_note-116) an atomic energy institute and the largest law firm in the country (Ryongnamsan Law Office).[[115]](Pyongyang#cite_note-117) Kim Il Sung University also has its own publishing house, sports club ([Ryongnamsan Sports Club](Ryongnamsan_Sports_Club "Ryongnamsan Sports Club")),[[116]](Pyongyang#cite_note-118) revolutionary museum, nature museum, libraries, a gym, indoor swimming pool and educator apartment houses. Its four main buildings were completed in 1965 (Building 1), 1972 (Building 2), and 2017 (Buildings 3 and 4).[[117]](Pyongyang#cite_note-119)[[118]](Pyongyang#cite_note-120)[[119]](Pyongyang#cite_note-121)

Other higher education establishments include [Kim Chaek University of Technology](Kim_Chaek_University_of_Technology "Kim Chaek University of Technology"), [Pyongyang University of Music and Dance](Pyongyang_University_of_Music_and_Dance "Pyongyang University of Music and Dance") and [Pyongyang University of Foreign Studies](Pyongyang_University_of_Foreign_Studies "Pyongyang University of Foreign Studies"). [Pyongyang University of Science and Technology (PUST)](Pyongyang_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Pyongyang University of Science and Technology") is the country's first private university where most of the lecturers are American and courses are carried out in English.[[120]](Pyongyang#cite_note-122)[[121]](Pyongyang#cite_note-123) A science and technology hall is under construction on Ssuk Islet. Its stated purpose is to contribute to the "informatization of educational resources" by centralizing teaching materials, compulsory literature and experimental data for state-level use in a digital format.[[122]](Pyongyang#cite_note-124)

<Sosong-guyok> hosts a 20 <MeV> [cyclotron](Cyclotron "Cyclotron") called MGC-20. The initial project was approved by the [International Atomic Energy Agency](International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") (IAEA) in 1983 and funded by the IAEA, the United States and the North Korean government. The cyclotron was ordered from the [Soviet Union](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") in 1985 and constructed between 1987 and 1990. It is used for student training, production of medical isotopes for [nuclear medicine](Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine") as well as studies in biology, chemistry and physics.[[123]](Pyongyang#cite_note-125)

**Ulaanbaatar** (/ˌuːlɑːn ˈbɑːtər/; [Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): Улаанбаатар, pronounced [ʊˌɮaːm‿ˈpaːʰtə̆r] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/6c/Mn-Ulaanbaatar.oga/Mn-Ulaanbaatar.oga.mp3)i, lit. (literal translation) "Red Hero"), previously anglicized as **Ulan Bator**, is the [capital](Capital_(political) "Capital (political)") and [most populous city](List_of_cities_in_Mongolia "List of cities in Mongolia") of <Mongolia>. It is the coldest capital city in the world by average yearly temperature.[[4]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-5) The municipality is located in north central Mongolia at an elevation of about 1,300 metres (4,300 ft) in a valley on the [Tuul River](Tuul_River "Tuul River"). The city was founded in 1639 as a nomadic [Buddhist](Buddhism_in_Mongolia "Buddhism in Mongolia") [monastic](Buddhist_monasticism "Buddhist monasticism") centre, changing location 28 times, and was permanently settled at its modern location in 1778.

During its early years, as **Örgöö** (anglicized as **Urga**), it became [Mongolia's](Mongolia_under_Qing_rule "Mongolia under Qing rule") preeminent religious centre and seat of the [Jebtsundamba Khutuktu](Jebtsundamba_Khutuktu "Jebtsundamba Khutuktu"), the spiritual head of the Gelug lineage of Tibetan Buddhism in Mongolia. Following the regulation of [Qing-Russian trade](Kyakhta_trade "Kyakhta trade") by the [Treaty of Kyakhta in 1727](Treaty_of_Kyakhta_(1727) "Treaty of Kyakhta (1727)"), a caravan route between <Beijing> and <Kyakhta> opened up, along which the city was eventually settled. With the collapse of the Qing Dynasty in 1911, the city was a focal point for independence efforts, leading to the [proclamation of the Bogd Khanate in 1911](Mongolian_Revolution_of_1911 "Mongolian Revolution of 1911") led by the [8th Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, or Bogd Khan](Bogd_Khan "Bogd Khan"), and again during the [communist revolution of 1921](Mongolian_Revolution_of_1921 "Mongolian Revolution of 1921"). With the proclamation of the [Mongolian People's Republic](Mongolian_People's_Republic "Mongolian People's Republic") in 1924, the city was officially renamed Ulaanbaatar and declared the country's capital. Modern urban planning began in the 1950s, with most of the old [ger districts](Ger_district "Ger district") replaced by [Soviet-style flats](Ugsarmal_bair "Ugsarmal bair"). In 1990, Ulaanbaatar was the site of large demonstrations that led to [Mongolia's transition to democracy and a market economy](Mongolian_Revolution_of_1990 "Mongolian Revolution of 1990"). Since 1990, an influx of migrants from the rest of the country has led to an explosive growth in its population, a major portion of whom live in ger districts, which has led to [harmful air pollution](Ulaanbaatar#Air_pollution) in winter.

Governed as an [independent municipality](Independent_city "Independent city"), Ulaanbaatar is surrounded by [Töv Province](T%C3%B6v_Province "Töv Province"), whose capital <Zuunmod> lies 43 kilometres (27 mi) south of the city. With a population of just over 1.6 million as of December 2022, it contains almost half of the country's total population.[[5]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-Statis.ub.gov.mn-6) As the country's [primate city](Primate_city "Primate city"), it serves as the cultural, industrial and financial heart as well as the center of its transport network,[[6]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-Official-7)

## Names and etymology

See also: [Names of Ulaanbaatar in different languages](Names_of_Ulaanbaatar_in_different_languages "Names of Ulaanbaatar in different languages")

The city at its establishment in 1639 was referred to as *Örgöö* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠥᠷᠭᠦᠭᠡ; Өргөө, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'Palace'). This name was eventually adapted as *Urga*[[7]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-8) in the West. By 1651, it began to be referred to as *Nomiĭn Khüree* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠨᠣᠮ ‍ᠤᠨ ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ; Номын хүрээ, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'Khüree of Wisdom'), and by 1706 it was referred to as *Ikh Khüree* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ; Их хүрээ, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'Great Khüree'). The Chinese equivalent, *Dà Kùlún* ([Chinese](Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 大庫倫, [Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): Да Хүрээ), was rendered into Western languages as *Kulun* or *Kuren*.

Other names include *[Bogdiin Khuree](Praise_of_Bogdiin_Khuree "Praise of Bogdiin Khuree")* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠪᠣᠭᠳᠠ ᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ; Богдын хүрээ, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'The [Bogd](Jebtsundamba_Khutuktu "Jebtsundamba Khutuktu")'s Khüree'), or simply *Khüree* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ; Хүрээ, romanized: *Küriye*), itself a term originally referring to an *enclosure* or *settlement*.

Upon [independence in 1911](Mongolian_Revolution_of_1911 "Mongolian Revolution of 1911"), with both the secular government and the [Bogd Khan](Bogd_Khan "Bogd Khan")'s palace present, the city's name was changed to *Niĭslel Khüree* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): ᠨᠡᠶᠢᠰᠯᠡᠯ ᠬᠦᠷᠢᠶᠡᠨ; Нийслэл Хүрээ, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'Capital Khüree').

When the city became the capital of the new [Mongolian People's Republic](Mongolian_People's_Republic "Mongolian People's Republic") in 1924, its name was changed to *Ulaanbaatar* (lit. (literal translation) 'Red Hero').

In the Western world, Ulaanbaatar continued to be generally known as Urga or Khuree until 1924, and afterward as Ulan Bator (a spelling derived from the Russian Улан-Батор). This form was defined two decades before the Mongolian name got its current [Cyrillic](Mongolian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet") spelling and transliteration (1941–1950); however, the name of the city was spelled *Ulaanbaatar koto* during the decade [in which Mongolia used the Latin alphabet](Mongolian_Latin_alphabet "Mongolian Latin alphabet").

Today, the city is referred to simply as *khot* ([Mongolian](Mongolian_language "Mongolian language"): хот, [lit.](Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'city'), as well as UB (*you-be*), from the English transliteration.

## History

Main article: [History of Ulaanbaatar](History_of_Ulaanbaatar "History of Ulaanbaatar")

### Prehistory

Human habitation at the site of Ulaanbaatar dates from the [Lower Paleolithic](Lower_Paleolithic "Lower Paleolithic"), with a number of sites on the [Bogd Khan](Bogd_Khan_Mountain "Bogd Khan Mountain"), Buyant-Ukhaa and Songinokhairkhan mountains, revealing tools which date from 300,000 years ago to 40,000–12,000 years ago. These [Upper Paleolithic](Upper_Paleolithic "Upper Paleolithic") people hunted [mammoth](Mammoth "Mammoth") and [woolly rhinoceros](Woolly_rhinoceros "Woolly rhinoceros"), the bones of which are found abundantly around Ulaanbaatar.

laanbaatar, including the tombs of Belkh Gorge near Dambadarjaalin monastery and tombs of Songinokhairkhan. Located on the banks of the [Tuul River](Tuul_River "Tuul River"), Ulaanbaatar has been well within the sphere of Turco-Mongol [nomadic empires](Nomadic_empires "Nomadic empires") throughout history.

[Wang Khan](Wang_Khan "Wang Khan"), Toghrul of the <Keraites>, a [Nestorian Christian](Church_of_the_East "Church of the East") monarch whom [Marco Polo](Marco_Polo "Marco Polo") identified as the legendary [Prester John](Prester_John "Prester John"), is said to have had his palace here (the Black Forest of the Tuul River) and forbade hunting in the holy mountain Bogd Uul. The palace is said to be where [Genghis Khan](Genghis_Khan "Genghis Khan") stayed with Yesui Khatun before attacking the [Tangut](Tangut_people "Tangut people") in 1226.

During the [Mongol Empire](Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire") (1206-1368) and [Northern Yuan Dynasty](Northern_Yuan "Northern Yuan") (1368-1635) the main, natural route from the capital region of <Karakorum> to the birthplace and tomb of the Khans in the Khentii mountain region ([Ikh Khorig](Ikh_Khorig "Ikh Khorig")) passed through the area of Ulaanbaatar. The Tuul River naturally leads to the north-side of Bogd Khan Mountain, which stands out as a large island of forest positioned conspicuously at the south-western edge of the Khentii mountains. As the main gate and stopover point on the route to and from the holy Khentii mountains, the Bogd Khan Mountain saw large amounts of traffic going past it and was protected from early times. Even after the Northern Yuan period it served as the location of the annual and triannual Assembly of Nobles (*Khan Uuliin Chuulgan*).

### Mobile monastery

Founded in 1639 as a [yurt](Yurt "Yurt") monastery, Ulaanbaatar, originally **Örgöö** (palace-[yurt](Yurt "Yurt")), was first located at Lake Shireet Tsagaan nuur (75 kilometres (47 miles) directly east of the imperial capital Karakorum) in what is now [Burd sum](B%C3%BCrd%2C_%C3%96v%C3%B6rkhangai "Bürd, Övörkhangai"), [Övörkhangai](%C3%96v%C3%B6rkhangai_Province "Övörkhangai Province"), around 230 kilometres (143 miles) south-west from the present site of Ulaanbaatar, and was intended by the Mongol nobles to be the seat of <Zanabazar>, the first [Jebtsundamba Khutughtu](Jebtsundamba_Khutughtu "Jebtsundamba Khutughtu"). Zanabazar returned to Mongolia from Tibet in 1651, and founded seven *aimags* (monastic departments) in Urga, later establishing four more.[[8]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-9)

As a mobile monastery-town, Örgöö was often moved to various places along the [Selenge](Selenga_River "Selenga River"), [Orkhon](Orkhon_River "Orkhon River") and Tuul rivers, as supply and other needs would demand. During the [Dzungar](Dzungar_Khanate "Dzungar Khanate") wars of the late 17th century, it was even moved to [Inner Mongolia](Inner_Mongolia "Inner Mongolia").[[9]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-10) As the city grew, it moved less and less.[[10]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-BH_of_UB-11)

The movements of the city can be detailed as follows: Shireet Tsagaan Nuur (1639), Khoshoo Tsaidam (1640), Khentii Mountains (1654), Ogoomor (1688), Inner Mongolia (1690), Tsetserlegiin Erdene Tolgoi (1700), Daagandel (1719), Usan Seer (1720), Ikh Tamir (1722), Jargalant (1723), Eeven Gol (1724), Khujirtbulan (1729), Burgaltai (1730), Sognogor (1732), Terelj (1733), Uliastai River (1734), Khui Mandal (1736), Khuntsal (1740), Udleg (1742), Ogoomor (1743), Selbe (1747), Uliastai River (1756), Selbe (1762), Khui Mandal (1772) and Selbe (1778).

In 1778, the city moved from Khui Mandal and settled for good at its current location, near the confluence of the Selbe and Tuul rivers, and beneath [Bogd Khan Uul](Bogd_Khan_Uul "Bogd Khan Uul"), at that time also on the caravan route from <Beijing> to <Kyakhta>.[[11]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-12)

One of the earliest Western mentions of Urga is the account of the Scottish traveller [John Bell](John_Bell_(traveller) "John Bell (traveller)") in 1721:
> What they call the Urga is the court, or the place where the prince (Tusheet Khan) and high priest (Bogd Jebtsundamba Khutugtu) reside, who are always encamped at no great distance from one another. They have several thousand tents about them, which are removed from time to time. The Urga is much frequented by merchants from China and Russia, and other places.[[12]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-13)

By Zanabazar's death in 1723, Urga was Mongolia's preeminent monastery in terms of religious authority. A council of seven of the highest-ranking [lamas](Lama "Lama") (*Khamba Nomon Khan*, *Ded Khamba* and five *Tsorj*) made most of the city's religious decisions. It had also become Outer Mongolia's commercial center. From 1733 to 1778, Urga moved around the vicinity of its present location. In 1754, the Erdene Shanzodba Yam **[^](Ulaanbaatar#ref_Administration_of_Ecclesiastical_Estate)** of Urga was given authority to supervise the administrative affairs of the Bogd's subjects. It also served as the city's chief judicial court. In 1758, the Qianlong Emperor appointed the [Khalkha](Khalkha_Mongols "Khalkha Mongols") Vice General Sanzaidorj as the first Mongol [amban](Amban "Amban") of Urga, with full authority to "oversee the Khuree and administer well all the Khutugtu's subjects".[[13]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-14)

In 1761, a second amban was appointed for the same purpose, a [Manchu](Manchu_people "Manchu people") one. A quarter-century later, in 1786, a decree issued in Peking gave right to the Urga ambans to decide the administrative affairs of [Tusheet Khan](T%C3%BCsheet_Khan "Tüsheet Khan") and Setsen Khan territories. With this, Urga became the highest civil authority in the country. Based on Urga's Mongol governor Sanzaidorj's petition, the [Qianlong Emperor](Qianlong_Emperor "Qianlong Emperor") officially recognized an annual ceremony on Bogd Khan Mountain in 1778 and provided the annual imperial donations. The city was the seat of the <Jebtsundamba> Khutugtus, two [Qing](Qing_Dynasty "Qing Dynasty") ambans, and a [Chinese](Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") trade town grew "four trees" 4.24 km (2.63 mi) east of the city center at the confluence of the Uliastai and Tuul rivers.

By 1778, Urga may have had as many as ten thousand monks, who were regulated by a monastic rule, Internal Rule of the Grand Monastery or *Yeke Kuriyen-u Doto'adu Durem*. For example, in 1797 a decree of the 4th Jebtsundamba forbade "singing, playing with archery, myagman, chess, usury and smoking"). Executions were forbidden where the holy temples of the Bogd Jebtsundama could be seen, so capital punishment took place away from the city.

In 1839, the 5th Bogd Jebtsundamba moved his residence to Gandan Hill, an elevated position to the west of the Baruun Damnuurchin markets. Part of the city was moved to nearby Tolgoit. In 1855, the part of the camp that moved to Tolgoit was brought back to its 1778 location, and the 7th Bogd Jebtsundamba returned to the Zuun Khuree. The [Gandan Monastery](Gandantegchinlen_Monastery "Gandantegchinlen Monastery") flourished as a center of philosophical studies.

### Urga and the Kyakhta trade

Following the [Treaty of Kyakhta](Treaty_of_Kyakhta "Treaty of Kyakhta") in 1727, Urga (Ulaanbaatar) was a major point of the [Kyakhta trade](Kyakhta_trade "Kyakhta trade") between Russia and China – mostly Siberian furs for Chinese cloth and later tea. The route ran south to Urga, southeast across the [Gobi Desert](Gobi_Desert "Gobi Desert") to <Kalgan>, and southeast over the mountains to Peking. Urga was also a collection point for goods coming from further west. These were either sent to China or shipped north to Russia via Kyakhta, because of legal restrictions and the lack of good trade routes to the west.

By 1908,[[14]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-15) there was a Russian quarter with a few hundred merchants and a Russian club and informal Russian mayor. East of the main town was the Russian consulate, built in 1863, with an [Orthodox](Russian_Orthodox_Church "Russian Orthodox Church") church, a post office and 20 [Cossack](Cossacks "Cossacks") guards. It was fortified in 1900 and briefly occupied by troops during the [Boxer Rebellion](Boxer_Rebellion "Boxer Rebellion"). There was a telegraph line north to Kyakhta and southeast to Kalgan and weekly postal service along these routes.

Beyond the Russian consulate was the Chinese trading post called [Maimaicheng](Bayanz%C3%BCrkh "Bayanzürkh"), and nearby the palace of the Manchu viceroy. With the growth of Western trade at the Chinese ports, the tea trade to Russia declined, some Chinese merchants left, and wool became the main export. Manufactured goods still came from Russia, but most were now brought from Kalgan by caravan. The annual trade was estimated at 25 million rubles, nine-tenths in Chinese hands and one-tenth in Russian.

The Moscow trade expedition of the 1910s estimated the population of Urga at 60,000, based on [Nikolay Przhevalsky](Nikolay_Przhevalsky "Nikolay Przhevalsky")'s study in the 1870s.[[15]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-archives.gov.mn-16)

The city's population swelled during the <Naadam> festival and major religious festivals to more than 100,000. In 1919, the number of monks had reached 20,000, up from 13,000 in 1810.[[15]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-archives.gov.mn-16)

On 29 December 1911, the [8th Jebtsundamba Khutughtu](Bogd_Khan "Bogd Khan") was declared ruler of an [independent Mongolia](Outer_Mongolia_(1911%E2%80%931919) "Outer Mongolia (1911–1919)") and assumed the title Bogd Khan.[[10]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-BH_of_UB-11) Khüree as the seat of the Jebtsundamba Khutugtu was the logical choice for the capital of the new state. However, following the [tripartite Kyakhta agreement of 1915](Treaty_of_Kyakhta_(1915) "Treaty of Kyakhta (1915)"), Mongolia's status was effectively reduced to mere autonomy.

In 1919, Mongolian nobles, over the opposition of the Bogd Khan, agreed with the Chinese resident Chen Yi on a settlement of the "Mongolian question" along Qing-era lines, but before this settlement could be put into effect, Khüree was occupied by the troops of Chinese warlord [Xu Shuzheng](Xu_Shuzheng "Xu Shuzheng"), who forced the Mongolian nobles and clergy to renounce autonomy completely.

The city changed hands twice in 1921. First, on 4 February, a mixed Russian/Mongolian force led by [White Russian](White_Movement "White Movement") warlord [Roman von Ungern-Sternberg](Roman_von_Ungern-Sternberg "Roman von Ungern-Sternberg") captured the city, freeing the [Bogd Khan](Bogd_Khan "Bogd Khan") from Chinese imprisonment and killing a part of the Chinese garrison. Baron Ungern's capture of Urga was followed by the clearing out of Mongolia's small gangs of demoralized Chinese soldiers and, at the same time, looting and murder of foreigners, including a vicious pogrom that [killed off the Jewish community](History_of_the_Jews_in_Mongolia "History of the Jews in Mongolia").[[16]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-17)[[17]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-18)[[18]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-By-19)

On 22 February 1921, the Bogd Khan was once again elevated to Great Khan of Mongolia in Urga.[[19]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-20) However, at the same time that Baron Ungern was taking control of Urga, a Soviet-supported Communist Mongolian force led by [Damdin Sükhbaatar](Damdin_S%C3%BCkhbaatar "Damdin Sükhbaatar") was forming in Russia, and in March they crossed the border. Ungern and his men rode out in May to meet Red Russian and Red Mongolian troops, but suffered a disastrous defeat in June.[[20]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-21)

In July 1921, the Communist Soviet-Mongolian army became the second conquering force in six months to enter Urga, and Mongolia came under the control of Soviet Russia. On 29 October 1924, the town was renamed *Ulaanbaatar*. On the session of the 1st Great People's Khuraldaan of Mongolia in 1924, a majority of delegates had expressed their wish to change the capital city's name to *[Baatar](Baghatur "Baghatur") Khot* ("Hero City"). However, under pressure from [Turar Ryskulov](Turar_Ryskulov "Turar Ryskulov"), a Kazakh Soviet activist of the [Communist International](Comintern "Comintern"), the city was named *Ulaanbaatar Khot* ("City of Red Hero").[[21]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-22)

### Socialist era

During the [socialist period](Socialist_Mongolia "Socialist Mongolia"), especially following the [Second World War](Second_World_War "Second World War"), most of the old [ger districts](Ger_district "Ger district") were replaced by [Soviet-style blocks of flats](Ugsarmal_bair "Ugsarmal bair"), often financed by the Soviet Union. [Urban planning](Urban_planning "Urban planning") began in the 1950s, and most of the city today is a result of construction between 1960 and 1985.[[22]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-23)

The [Trans-Mongolian Railway](Trans-Mongolian_Railway "Trans-Mongolian Railway"), connecting Ulaanbaatar with Moscow and Beijing, was completed in 1956, and cinemas, theaters, museums and other modern facilities were erected. Most of the temples and monasteries of pre-socialist Khüree were destroyed following the anti-religious [purges](Stalinist_purges_in_Mongolia "Stalinist purges in Mongolia") of the late 1930s. The Gandan monastery was reopened in 1944 when the [U.S. Vice President](Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") [Henry Wallace](Henry_A._Wallace "Henry A. Wallace") asked to see a monastery during his visit to Mongolia.

### Democratic protests of 1989–1990

Ulaanbaatar was a major site of demonstrations that led to Mongolia's [transition to democracy and market economy in 1990](Mongolian_Revolution_of_1990 "Mongolian Revolution of 1990"). On 10 December 1989, protesters outside the Youth Culture Center called for Mongolia to implement [perestroika](Perestroika "Perestroika") and [glasnost](Glasnost "Glasnost") in their full sense. Dissident leaders demanded free elections and economic reform. On 14 January 1990, the protesters, having grown from two hundred to over a thousand, met at the Lenin Museum in Ulaanbaatar. A demonstration in Sükhbaatar Square on 21 January followed. Afterwards, weekend demonstrations were held in January and February, accompanied by the forming of Mongolia's first opposition parties.

On 7 March, ten dissidents assembled in Sükhbaatar Square and went on a hunger strike. Thousands of supporters joined them. More arrived the following day and the crowd grew more unruly. 71 people were injured, one fatally. On 9 March, the Communist [Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party](Mongolian_People's_Party "Mongolian People's Party") (MPRP) government resigned. The provisional government announced Mongolia's first free elections, which were held in July. The [MPRP](Mongolian_People's_Party "Mongolian People's Party") won the election and resumed power.[[23]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-24)

### Since 1990

Since Mongolia's transition to a market economy in 1990, the city has experienced further growth—especially in the ger districts, as construction of new blocks of flats had basically slowed to a halt in the 1990s. The population has more than doubled to over one million inhabitants. The rapid growth has caused a number of social, environmental and transportation problems. In recent years, construction of new buildings has gained new momentum, especially in the city center, and apartment prices have skyrocketed.

In 2008, [Ulaanbaatar was the scene of riots](2008_riot_in_Mongolia "2008 riot in Mongolia") after the [Mongolian Democratic](Democratic_Party_(Mongolia) "Democratic Party (Mongolia)"), [Civic Will Party](Civic_Will_Party "Civic Will Party") and [Republican](Republican_Party_(Mongolia) "Republican Party (Mongolia)") parties disputed the [Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party](Mongolian_People's_Party "Mongolian People's Party")'s victory in the [parliamentary elections](Mongolian_legislative_election%2C_2008 "Mongolian legislative election, 2008"). A four-day state of emergency was declared, the capital was placed under a 22:00-to-08:00 curfew, and alcohol sales banned;[[24]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-BBC2-25) following these measures, rioting did not resume.[[25]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-BBC3-26) This was the first deadly riot in modern Ulaanbaatar's history.

In April 2013, Ulaanbaatar hosted the 7th Ministerial Conference of the [Community of Democracies](Community_of_Democracies "Community of Democracies"), and has also lent its name to the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on Northeast Asian Security.

#### Demolition of historic buildings

In October 2019, one of the oldest structures in Ulaanbaatar, the wooden building that housed the Victims of Political Persecution Memorial Museum, was demolished.[[26]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-Menarndt-27) The 2019 Mongolian government budget furthermore included items for the demolition of a number of historic neoclassical buildings in the heart of Ulaanbaatar, including the [Natural History Museum](Mongolian_Natural_History_Museum "Mongolian Natural History Museum"), [Opera and Ballet House](National_Academic_Theatre_of_Opera_and_Ballet_of_Mongolia "National Academic Theatre of Opera and Ballet of Mongolia"), Drama Theatre and Central Library.[[27]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-28) The decision was met by a public outcry and criticism from the Union of Mongolian Architects, which demanded that the buildings be preserved and restored.[[28]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-29) Despite daily sit-ins by protesters, the Natural History Museum was duly demolished. In January 2020, culture minister Yondonperenlein Baatarbileg denied that the government intended to demolish the other buildings and stated that the government planned to renovate them instead.[[29]](Ulaanbaatar#cite_note-30)

## Geography

Ulaanbaatar is located at about 1,350 metres (4,430 ft) above mean [sea level](Sea_level "Sea level"), slightly east of the center of Mongolia, on the Tuul River, a sub-[tributary](Tributary "Tributary") of the [Selenge](Selenga "Selenga"), in a valley at the foot of the mountain [Bogd Khan Uul](Bogd_Khan_Uul "Bogd Khan Uul"). Bogd Khan Uul is a broad, heavily forested mountain rising 2,250 metres (7,380 ft) to the south of Ulaanbaatar. It forms the boundary between the [steppe](Steppe "Steppe") zone to the south and the forest-steppe zone to the north.

The forests of the mountains surrounding Ulaanbaatar are composed of evergreen pines, [deciduous](Deciduous "Deciduous") larches and [birches](Birch "Birch"), while the riverine forest of the Tuul River is composed of broad-leaved, deciduous [poplars](Populus "Populus"), [elms](Elm "Elm") and [willows](Willow "Willow"). Ulaanbaatar lies at roughly the same latitude as <Vienna>, <Munich>, [Orléans](Orl%C3%A9ans "Orléans") and <Seattle>. It lies at roughly the same longitude as <Chongqing>, <Hanoi> and <Jakarta>.

content.content: I found exactly what I was looking for! According to the Wikipedia article "List of Mongolian provinces by GDP", Ulaanbaatar's GDP per capita in PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) is **$17,508 USD** (as of 2020 data). This is listed in the table "Provinces by GDP per capita" where Ulaanbaatar ranks 2nd among Mongolian provinces with a GDP per capita of $17,508 USD (PPP), which is 140.5% of the national average.

content:
Based on my research of the Wikipedia article "List of Mongolian provinces by GDP," I found the information you're looking for.

**Ulaanbaatar's GDP per capita (PPP): $17,508 USD**

This data is from 2020 according to the National Statistics Office of Mongolia. In this ranking:
- Ulaanbaatar ranks **2nd** among Mongolia's 22 provinces/regions
- This represents **140.5%** of Mongolia's national average GDP per capita (PPP)
- The national average GDP per capita (PPP) for Mongolia in 2020 was $12,463 USD

This makes Ulaanbaatar one of the wealthiest regions in Mongolia economically, which makes sense given that it's the country's capital, financial center, and home to almost half of Mongolia's total population. The city contributes **64.58%** of the country's total GDP despite having less than 50% of the population.

For comparison, the only province with a higher GDP per capita (PPP) is Orkhon Province at $19,255 USD.

**Taipei** (臺北 /ˌtaɪˈpeɪ/ [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ee/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Vealhurl-Taipei.wav/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Vealhurl-Taipei.wav.mp3)i),[[2]](Taipei#cite_note-3) officially **Taipei City**,[[upper-roman 1]](Taipei#cite_note-word1-1) is the [capital](Capital_city "Capital city")[[lower-alpha 1]](Taipei#cite_note-7) and a [special municipality](Special_municipality_(Taiwan) "Special municipality (Taiwan)") of <Taiwan>.[[5]](Taipei#cite_note-gov-6)[[6]](Taipei#cite_note-8) Located in [Northern Taiwan](Regions_of_Taiwan "Regions of Taiwan"), Taipei City is an [enclave](Enclave "Enclave") of New Taipei that sits about 25 km (16 mi) southwest of the northern port city of Keelung. Most of the city rests on the [Taipei Basin](Taipei_Basin "Taipei Basin"), an ancient lakebed. The basin is bounded by the relatively narrow valleys of the [Keelung](Keelung_River "Keelung River") and [Xindian rivers](Xindian_River "Xindian River"), which join to form the [Tamsui River](Tamsui_River "Tamsui River") along the city's western border.[[7]](Taipei#cite_note-tcggeo-9)

The name "Taipei" can refer either to the whole metropolitan area or just the municipality alone. In English-language news reports, the name *Taipei* often serves as a [synecdoche](Synecdoche "Synecdoche") referring to central government of Taiwan. Due to the ambiguous [political status of Taiwan](Political_status_of_Taiwan "Political status of Taiwan") internationally, the term *[Chinese Taipei](Chinese_Taipei "Chinese Taipei")* is also frequently used as a [synonym](Synonym "Synonym") for the entire country, as when Taiwan's governmental representatives participate in [international organizations](International_organizations "International organizations") or Taiwan's athletes compete in international sporting events, including the [Olympics](Olympic_Games "Olympic Games").

## Names

See also: [Chinese language romanization in Taiwan](Chinese_language_romanization_in_Taiwan "Chinese language romanization in Taiwan")

The spellings *Taipei* and *Tʻai-pei* derive from the [Wade–Giles](Wade%E2%80%93Giles "Wade–Giles") romanization *Tʻai²-pei³*[[12]](Taipei#cite_note-15) which means *the North of Taiwan* in Chinese. The name could be also romanized as *Táiběi* according to [Hanyu Pinyin](Hanyu_Pinyin "Hanyu Pinyin") and [Tongyong Pinyin](Tongyong_Pinyin "Tongyong Pinyin").[[13]](Taipei#cite_note-16)[[14]](Taipei#cite_note-17)[[15]](Taipei#cite_note-18)

The city has also been known as *Tai-pak*[[16]](Taipei#cite_note-19)[[17]](Taipei#cite_note-20) (derived from [Taiwanese Hokkien](Taiwanese_Hokkien "Taiwanese Hokkien")) and *Taipeh*.[[18]](Taipei#cite_note-21)[[19]](Taipei#cite_note-22)

During the [Japanese rule](Taiwan_under_Japanese_rule "Taiwan under Japanese rule"), Taipei was known as *Taihoku*, which is the pronunciation of the [Chinese characters](Chinese_characters "Chinese characters") (<Kanji>) for Taipei in Japanese.[[20]](Taipei#cite_note-23)

## History

Main article: [History of Taipei](History_of_Taipei "History of Taipei")

See also: [North-South divide in Taiwan § Taipei](North-South_divide_in_Taiwan "North-South divide in Taiwan")

Prior to the significant influx of Han Chinese colonists, the region of [Taipei Basin](Taipei_Basin "Taipei Basin") was mainly inhabited by the [plains aborigines](Taiwanese_plains_aborigines "Taiwanese plains aborigines") called <Ketagalan>. The number of Han colonists gradually increased in the early 18th century under [Qing Dynasty rule](Taiwan_under_Qing_rule "Taiwan under Qing rule") after the government began permitting development in the area.[[21]](Taipei#cite_note-24) In 1875, the northern part of the island was incorporated into the new [Taipeh Prefecture](Taipeh_Prefecture "Taipeh Prefecture").

It was formerly established as Taipeh-fu and was the temporary capital of the island in 1887 when it was declared a province ([Fukien-Taiwan Province](Taiwan_Province#Qing_Dynasty "Taiwan Province")).[[22]](Taipei#cite_note-25)[[23]](Taipei#cite_note-26) Taipeh was formally made the provincial capital in 1894. The romanized transcription of Taipeh was changed to Taihoku in 1895 when the Empire of Japan annexed Taiwan, based on the Japanese reading of the two characters. The writing in Chinese characters remained unaltered. Under Japanese rule, the city was administered under [Taihoku Prefecture](Taihoku_Prefecture "Taihoku Prefecture"). Taiwan's Japanese rulers embarked on an extensive program of advanced [urban planning](Urban_planning "Urban planning") that featured extensive railroad links. A number of Taipei landmarks and cultural institutions date from this period.[[24]](Taipei#cite_note-marsh1-27)

Following the [surrender of Japan](Surrender_of_Japan "Surrender of Japan") to the [Allies](Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") during 1945, effective control of Taiwan was [handed to the Republic of China (ROC)](History_of_Taiwan_since_1945 "History of Taiwan since 1945"). After facing defeat from Communist forces, the ruling <Kuomintang> relocated the [ROC government](Government_of_the_Republic_of_China "Government of the Republic of China") to Taiwan and declared Taipei the [provisional capital](Provisional_capital "Provisional capital") of the ROC in December 1949.[[25]](Taipei#cite_note-ng-28)[[26]](Taipei#cite_note-bbctimeline-retreat-29)[[27]](Taipei#cite_note-30) Taiwan's Kuomintang rulers regarded the city as the capital of [Taiwan Province](Taiwan_Province "Taiwan Province") and their control as mandated by [General Order No. 1](General_Order_No._1 "General Order No. 1").

In 1990, Taipei provided the backdrop for the [Wild Lily student rallies](Wild_Lily_student_movement "Wild Lily student movement") that moved Taiwanese society from one-party rule to multi-party [democracy](Democracy "Democracy") by [1996](1996_Taiwan_presidential_election "1996 Taiwan presidential election"). The city has ever since served as the seat of Taiwan's democratically elected national government.

### Early settlers–Qing dynasty

The region known as the [Taipei Basin](Taipei_Basin "Taipei Basin") was home to [Ketagalan](Ketagalan_people "Ketagalan people") tribes before the eighteenth century.[[28]](Taipei#cite_note-31) [Han Chinese](Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") colonists from [Dabu County](Dabu_County "Dabu County"), [Yongding County](Yongding_County "Yongding County"), [Anxi](Anxi_County "Anxi County") and <Tong'an> of [Southern Fujian](Southern_Fujian "Southern Fujian") began to settle in the Taipei Basin in 1709.[[29]](Taipei#cite_note-kelly-32)[[30]](Taipei#cite_note-tcghistory-33)

In the late 19th century, the Taipei area, where the major Han Chinese settlements in northern Taiwan and one of the designated overseas trade ports, [Tamsui](Tamsui_District "Tamsui District"), were located, gained economic importance due to the booming overseas trade, especially that of [tea](Tea "Tea") export. In 1875, the northern part of Taiwan was separated from [Taiwan Prefecture](Taiwan_Prefecture "Taiwan Prefecture") and incorporated into the new [Taipeh Prefecture](Taipeh_Prefecture "Taipeh Prefecture") as a new administrative entity of the Qing dynasty.[[24]](Taipei#cite_note-marsh1-27) Having been established adjoining the flourishing townships of [Bangka](Wanhua_District "Wanhua District"), <Dalongdong>, and <Twatutia>, the new prefectural capital was known as *Chengnei* ([Chinese](Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 城內; [pinyin](Pinyin "Pinyin"): *chéngnèi*; [Pe̍h-ōe-jī](Pe%CC%8Dh-%C5%8De-j%C4%AB "Pe̍h-ōe-jī"): *siâⁿ-lāi*), "the inner city", and government buildings were erected there. From 1875 until the beginning of Japanese rule in 1895, Taipei was part of Tamsui County of Taipeh Prefecture and the prefectural capital.[[31]](Taipei#cite_note-34)

In 1885, as work commenced to govern the island as a province, Taipeh was thus temporarily designated as a provincial capital. The city officially became the capital in 1894. Nowadays, all that remains from the historical period is the north gate. The west gate and [city walls](Taipei_City_Walls "Taipei City Walls") were demolished by the Japanese while the south gate, little south gate, and east gate were extensively modified by the <Kuomintang> and have lost much of their original character.[[32]](Taipei#cite_note-35)

### Empire of Japan

As settlement for losing the [First Sino-Japanese War](First_Sino-Japanese_War "First Sino-Japanese War"), China ceded the [island of Taiwan](Island_of_Taiwan "Island of Taiwan") to the [Empire of Japan](Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") in 1895 as part of the [Treaty of Shimonoseki](Treaty_of_Shimonoseki "Treaty of Shimonoseki"). After the Japanese takeover, Taipei, romanized into English as **Taihoku** following the Japanese language pronunciation, was retained as the capital. It subsequently emerged as the political center of the Japanese Colonial Government.[[24]](Taipei#cite_note-marsh1-27) During that time the city acquired the characteristics of an administrative center, including many new public buildings and [housing for civil servants](Qidong_Street_Japanese_Houses "Qidong Street Japanese Houses"). Much of the architecture of Taipei dates from the period of [Japanese rule](Taiwan_under_Japanese_rule "Taiwan under Japanese rule"), including the [Presidential Office Building](Presidential_Office_Building_(Republic_of_China) "Presidential Office Building (Republic of China)") which was the Office of the [Governor-General of Taiwan](Governor-General_of_Taiwan "Governor-General of Taiwan").

During Japanese rule, Taihoku was incorporated in 1920 as part of [Taihoku Prefecture](Taihoku_Prefecture "Taihoku Prefecture"). It included [Bangka](Wanhua_District "Wanhua District"), <Twatutia>, and *Jōnai* (城內) among other small settlements. The eastern village of *Matsuyama* (松山庄, modern-day [Songshan District, Taipei](Songshan_District%2C_Taipei "Songshan District, Taipei")) was annexed into Taihoku City in 1938. Taihoku and surrounding areas were bombed by Allied forces on several occasions. The largest of these Allied air raids, the [Taihoku Air Raid](Taihoku_Air_Raid "Taihoku Air Raid"), took place on 31 May 1945.
